topics.title: METAR / SPECI decoding
lesson: A METAR is the routine hourly aerodrome weather report. A SPECI is a special report issued between hours when conditions change significantly. This is the Canadian format. Always confirm details against the current Manual of Surface Weather Observations (MANOBS) and your course material.

lesson.formula: METAR CYHZ 261200Z 27015G25KT 15SM -RA BKN020 OVC060 08/06 A2985 RMK SC6AC2 SLP112

list: Station: ICAO identifier (CYHZ is Halifax Stanfield).
Date and time: day of month and UTC time (261200Z is the 26th at 1200 UTC).
Wind: a two-minute mean. Direction in degrees TRUE (to the nearest 10), speed in knots, gusts after G (27015G25KT). 00000KT is calm. VRB means variable.
Visibility: statute miles in Canada, with fractions (1/2SM, 1 1/2SM).
Present weather: intensity (- light, + heavy, no symbol for moderate), then type (RA, SN, FG, BR, TS...).

Cloud: amount and height in hundreds of feet, measured from the aerodrome level at airports (BKN020 is broken at 2,000 ft). Amounts: FEW (more than 0 to 2 oktas), SCT (3 to 4), BKN (5 to 7), OVC (8), SKC (no cloud).
Temperature and dew point in whole degrees C. M means minus (M03/M05 is -3 and -5).
Altimeter: A followed by inches of mercury without the decimal (A2985 is 29.85).

Remarks (RMK): extra detail such as cloud layers in oktas (SC6AC2) and sea level pressure (SLP112 is 1011.2 hPa). To decode: if the three digits start with 7, 8 or 9, put a 9 in front; if they start with 0, 1, 2 or 3, put 10 in front (SLP134 is 1013.4 hPa).
Ceiling: height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility when the sky is obscured.
VV003: obscured sky with vertical visibility of 300 ft.

lesson.note: METAR and SPECI winds are in degrees true. Always check whether a wind source is true or magnetic before using it for a runway.

terms: Special report issued when conditions change significantly between routine METARs.
Lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility.
Eighths of the sky covered by cloud.

questions.q: In a METAR, what does 'M03/M05' mean?
c: Temperature -3 C, dew point -5 C
Temperature 3 C, dew point 5 C
Temperature -5 C, dew point -3 C
Mist at 3 and 5 km
questions.e: M indicates a negative value. The first number is temperature, the second is dew point.

questions.q: Wind direction in a METAR is referenced to:
c: True north
Magnetic north
Grid north
Runway heading
questions.e: MANOBS 3.2.1: wind direction is reported with respect to true north in METAR and SPECI.

questions.q: What does 'VV003' mean?
c: Obscured sky with a vertical visibility of 300 ft
Visibility 3 miles with variable winds at 3 kt
Few clouds at 300 ft above ground with good visibility
Variable wind direction of 003 degrees at low speed
questions.e: VV indicates vertical visibility into an obscured sky, in hundreds of feet.

questions.q: An altimeter group reads A2992. What does that mean?
c: 29.92 inches of mercury
2992 hectopascals at sea level
A pressure altitude of 2,992 feet
Visibility of 2.9 miles with cloud at 2,000 ft
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: the letter A prefixes the 4-digit group, which is inches of mercury; A2992 is 29.92 inHg.

questions.q: What defines the ceiling?
c: The lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility
The lowest cloud layer reported at any amount, including few
The highest broken or overcast layer reported by the observer
The average height of all the cloud layers in the observation
questions.e: MANOBS 7.2.7: ceiling is the lowest layer aloft reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or the vertical visibility (VV). FEW and SCT layers do not constitute a ceiling.

questions.q: In a METAR, what does the group 'BKN012' mean?
c: Broken cloud layer with base at 1,200 ft
Broken cloud layer with base at 12,000 ft
Few clouds at 120 ft
Overcast at 1,200 m
questions.e: Heights are in hundreds of feet. At airports they are measured from the official aerodrome level (MANOBS 7.3.1). 012 = 1,200 ft.

questions.q: What does '18015G25KT' report?
c: Wind from 180 degrees at 15 kt, gusting 25 kt
Wind from 150 degrees at 18 kt, gusting 25 kt
Wind toward 180 degrees at 15 kt
Wind from 180 degrees at 25 kt, gusting 15 kt
questions.e: Direction (3 digits), speed (2 digits), G, gust, then unit.

questions.q: A METAR shows temperature/dew point group '03/M01'. What are the values?
c: Temperature +3 C, dew point -1 C
Temperature -3 C, dew point +1 C
Temperature +3 C, dew point +1 C
Temperature 3 C, dew point 0 C
questions.e: The M prefix means minus.

questions.q: Which group in a METAR shows the altimeter setting in inches of mercury?
c: RMK
CAVOK
questions.e: In Canada and the US, altimeter is reported as A followed by four digits.

questions.q: What does 'VRB05KT' indicate?
c: Variable wind direction at 5 kt
Wind from 050 degrees at 5 kt
Calm winds
Wind from the north at 5 kt
questions.e: VRB is used for light, variable winds.

questions.q: A SPECI is issued when:
c: Significant changes meet specified criteria between routine reports
Every hour on the hour, whatever the weather at the station
Only at midnight, when the observer changes shift
Only when winds exceed 50 kt at the observing site
questions.e: SPECI reports are special reports after significant changes.

sources: MANOBS 8th ed. Amendment 3: 2.5 (METAR and SPECI), 3.2.1 (wind, two-minute mean, true), 4.5.1 (visibility in SM), 7.2.7 (ceiling), 7.3.1 (cloud reference level)
NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): METAR decode, oktas ranges, M prefix, A group in inHg, intensity qualifiers, SLP decoding
Transport Canada AIM MET 1.2.1: METARs hourly on the hour
unverified: The SPECI criteria list (MANOBS 11.2.3) could not be opened with the tools used, so the lesson only says SPECIs are issued when conditions cross specified criteria.
Whether tower and ATIS winds are magnetic was not confirmed in a Canadian publication, so that statement was removed.

topics.title: TAF decoding and amendment criteria
lesson: A TAF is an aerodrome forecast. It applies to conditions within 5 nautical miles of the centre of the runway complex, depending on local terrain. TAFs are prepared four times daily with a validity of up to 30 hours. Issue times vary by site (they are listed in the CFS), and the next issue time is stated at the end of each TAF. Check current MANAIR and AIM for exact details.

lesson.formula:
TAF CYHZ 261140Z 2612/2712 27012KT P6SM FEW040 SCT100
  FM261800 29015G25KT P6SM SCT040
  BECMG 2700/2702 31008KT
  TEMPO 2703/2706 3SM -SHRA BKN015

list: Issue time (261140Z) and valid period (2612/2712: from 1200 UTC on the 26th to 1200 UTC on the 27th).
FM (from): a rapid, permanent change written FM followed by day, hour and minute (FM300130). All forecast elements must be restated, and the new forecast replaces everything before it.
BECMG (becoming): a permanent change expected over one to four hours, written as a period (BECMG 2906/2908). After the period, the new conditions persist until changed again.
TEMPO (temporary): temporary fluctuations lasting less than an hour at a time and, in total, no more than half the stated period (TEMPO 1306/1312). TEMPO does not change the wind or wind shear.
PROB30 or PROB40: the probability that the stated conditions occur during the period. It is not the fraction of the time they last. PROB does not change the wind or wind shear.

lesson: P6SM means visibility greater than 6 statute miles. NSW (no significant weather) can be used when significant weather is no longer expected. VV is vertical visibility for an obscured sky.

An amended TAF is marked TAF AMD. Per the Transport Canada AIM, forecasts are amended when significant changes in ceiling or visibility occur, and also for significant changes in wind or present weather. They are also amended when freezing precipitation begins or is expected, even if it was not forecast. The exact thresholds are in MANAIR Chapter 2.

lesson.note: When decoding, read the base forecast first, then apply each change group in order. A validity period that ends at midnight UTC is coded 24 (2912/2924); one that begins at midnight is coded 00 (3000/3018). For alternate planning, a TAF with BECMG or TEMPO must meet alternate minima, while PROB conditions need only meet landing minima (NAV CANADA guide).

terms: From: abrupt, complete change from the stated time.
Becoming: permanent change expected over one to four hours.
Temporary: fluctuations under one hour at a time, no more than half the period in total.

questions.q: What does an FM group in a TAF indicate?
c: A rapid change with a new complete forecast from the stated time
A gradual change that develops slowly during the stated period
A short-lived fluctuation that returns to the previous conditions
A probability forecast that applies for the next six hours only
questions.e: FM replaces all previous conditions starting at the stated time.

questions.q: What does BECMG mean?
c: A gradual change during the stated period
A sudden change that replaces all earlier groups
A brief fluctuation lasting under an hour each time
A probability of change between thirty and forty percent
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: BECMG is a permanent change expected over one to four hours. After the period the new conditions persist.

questions.q: What does TEMPO indicate?
c: Temporary fluctuations, each lasting less than an hour
A permanent change
A change that always lasts more than 2 hours
A reduction in visibility only
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: TEMPO fluctuations last under one hour at a time and cover no more than half the forecast period. TEMPO does not change wind.

questions.q: What does P6SM mean in a TAF?
c: Visibility greater than 6 statute miles
Visibility less than 6 statute miles in precipitation
A six percent probability of reduced visibility
Pressure falling six hectopascals in the next hour
questions.e: P means plus, so more than 6 statute miles.

questions.q: What area does a TAF cover?
c: The area within about 5 NM of the aerodrome
The entire province in which the aerodrome is located
An area of about 100 NM around the aerodrome
Only the runway surface and its immediate approach lights
questions.e: AIM MET 3.1: TAFs relate to conditions within 5 NM of the centre of the runway complex, depending on local terrain.

questions.q: A TAF valid period of '2412/2512' covers:
c: 1200 UTC on the 24th to 1200 UTC on the 25th
2400 UTC on the 12th to 2500 UTC on the 12th
1200 UTC on the 12th to 1200 UTC on the 25th
24 hours starting at local noon
questions.e: The format is DDHH/DDHH in UTC. A period ending at midnight UTC is coded 24 (for example 2912/2924).

questions.q: What does 'TEMPO' in a TAF indicate?
c: Temporary fluctuations lasting less than one hour at a time, under half the period
A permanent change that lasts for the rest of the valid period
A change with a 50% probability of occurring in the period
The cancellation of the forecast and its replacement
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: TEMPO is used when the condition lasts under one hour at a time and covers no more than half the period.

questions.q: What does 'BECMG' mean?
c: A gradual change to new conditions
A temporary change lasting less than an hour at a time
A calm period with winds below 3 kt at the airport
An amendment to the forecast issued after a major change
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: BECMG is a permanent change expected over one to four hours.

questions.q: 'PROB30' in a TAF signals:
c: A 30% probability of the stated conditions
A 30-minute delay before the change in conditions begins
A wind speed of 30 kt in the stated period
A visibility of 30 km in the stated period
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: PROB30 or PROB40 is the probability that the condition occurs during the period, not the fraction of time it lasts.

questions.q: An amendment (AMD) is issued when:
c: Forecast conditions no longer represent expected weather
At the start of each new valid period in the forecast
At random times chosen by the forecaster on shift
Only when winds at the airport are calm for an hour
questions.e: AIM MET 3.1: TAFs are amended when significant changes in ceiling or visibility occur, and also for significant changes in wind or present weather.

questions.q: TAF cloud and visibility values are expressed:
c: In a similar manner to METAR
In metres and kilometres, unlike the METAR format
In kilometres only, with cloud in metres above sea level
In inches of mercury for pressure and feet for visibility
questions.e: TAF uses the same codes as METAR for wind, visibility and cloud.

sources: Transport Canada AIM MET 1.3.3 and 3.1: 5 NM radius, four times daily, up to 30 hours, amendment rules
NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): FM, BECMG, TEMPO, PROB, P6SM, NSW, VV, 2400/0000 coding, alternate minima, header and period examples
unverified: MANAIR Chapter 2 (the full TAF standards and amendment thresholds) could not be opened with the tools used.

topics.title: Surface analysis and prognostic charts
lesson: A surface analysis chart shows the observed pattern of pressure, fronts and weather at a fixed time. A prognostic chart ('prog') shows the forecast pattern at a future time.

list: Isobars: lines of equal sea level pressure, analysed at 4 hPa intervals from a 1000 hPa reference value. The national surface analysis is produced four times a day, valid 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC. Tight spacing means strong winds. Labels often show only the last two digits (for example 96 is 996 hPa, 04 is 1004 hPa).
H and L: high and low centres, with central pressure.
Fronts: cold (blue line with barbs), warm (red line with half circles), occluded (usually purple) and stationary (usually alternating red and blue). Check the legend on your chart.
Troughs and ridges: lines of curvature of the isobars.
Station models: plotted observations at each station.
Temperature: upper left. Dew point: lower left.
Pressure: upper right, in tenths of hPa with the leading digit dropped (132 means 1013.2; 987 means 998.7).
Pressure tendency: lower right.
Sky cover: the circle at the centre, filled by the amount of cloud cover.
Wind barb: the staff points toward the direction the wind comes from. Each full barb is 10 kt, half barb 5 kt, pennant (triangle) 50 kt.

lesson: Isobar spacing gives a rough guide to wind speed. Winds blow roughly parallel to the isobars, slightly across them toward lower pressure near the surface. Low pressure on the left in the Northern Hemisphere.

lesson.note: A prog is a model-based forecast reviewed by a forecaster. Compare the prog with the latest analysis to check how well the model captured the current situation.

terms: Chart of observed conditions at a specific time.
Prognostic chart: forecast of future conditions.
Standard arrangement of plotted weather elements around a station.

questions.q: What does closely spaced isobars on a surface chart indicate?
c: Strong winds
Weak winds
A cold front only
Clear skies
questions.e: Closer spacing means a steeper pressure gradient.

questions.q: A station model shows pressure '132'. What is the sea level pressure?
c: 132 hPa
1132 hPa
questions.e: The leading 10 is dropped, so 132 means 1013.2 hPa.

questions.q: On a wind barb, what does a pennant (triangle) represent?
c: 50 kt
10 kt
5 kt
100 kt
questions.e: A pennant is 50 kt, a full barb 10 kt, and a half barb 5 kt.

questions.q: What is a prognostic chart?
c: A forecast chart of expected conditions
A chart of observed conditions
A satellite picture
A radar image
questions.e: Progs show forecast fronts, pressure and weather at a future time.

questions.q: On a wind barb, to which direction does the staff point?
c: The direction the wind is coming from
The direction the wind is going to
North always
The nearest low pressure
questions.e: Wind direction is always where the wind comes from.

questions.q: On a surface analysis, closely spaced isobars indicate:
c: Strong winds
Light winds
No wind
Fog
questions.e: Tight pressure gradient means strong wind.

questions.q: An H on the chart denotes:
c: A centre of high pressure
A hurricane with sustained winds above 64 kt
A maximum of humidity at the surface in the warm sector
A region of hail reported in the last hour
questions.e: H marks high-pressure centres.

questions.q: Isobars on a surface chart are usually drawn every:
c: 4 hPa
50 hPa
0.1 hPa
100 hPa
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: isobars are analysed at 4 hPa intervals from a 1000 hPa reference value.

questions.q: A prog chart shows:
c: The forecast positions of systems and weather
Past weather only, as observed during the last six hours
Radar echoes and lightning strikes for the last hour
Station models only, with no forecast information
questions.e: Prognostic charts show the expected future state.

questions.q: On a Canadian surface analysis, how is a warm front drawn?
c: As a red line with half circles
As a blue line with barbs
As a dashed black line with no symbols
As a purple line with half circles and barbs
questions.e: NAV CANADA guide: fronts are shown as blue lines with barbs (cold front) or red lines with half circles (warm front).

questions.q: A station model's wind barb shows direction from:
c: The shaft pointing toward where the wind blows from
The shaft pointing toward where the wind is going
The flags only, with the shaft showing the speed
The dots at the end, which point in the wind direction
questions.e: The shaft points into the wind.

sources: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): isobars at 4 hPa from 1000 hPa, analysis times, cold and warm front symbols, SLP decoding rule
unverified: Occluded and stationary front colours, the dashed trough line, the last-two-digits isobar labels and the station model layout are common charting practice, not confirmed in a fetched source.
The NAV CANADA guide's symbol pages are images, so line styles could not be read.

topics.title: Upper-air charts (850, 700, 500, 250 hPa)
lesson: Upper-air charts are drawn for constant pressure levels, prepared twice daily at 00 and 12 UTC. They show geopotential height (the height at which that pressure is found), temperature, dew point depression and wind.

list: 850 hPa (about 1,500 m, 5,000 ft ASL): low-level temperature and moisture. Warm and cold advection, the 0 C line, low-level jets, and rain versus snow guidance.
700 hPa (about 3,000 m, 10,000 ft ASL): mid-level moisture and ascent. Cloud layers, steering of low-level systems, and the capping inversion for convection.
500 hPa (about 5,500 m, 18,000 ft ASL): the main steering level. Troughs, ridges, vorticity, and cut-off lows. Closely spaced contours mean strong winds.
250 hPa (about 10,400 m, 34,000 ft ASL) and nearby 300 hPa (about 9,000 m): jet streams, upper divergence, tropopause-level features. Isotachs show wind speed maxima.
Height contours (in decametres, dam). Flow is parallel to the contours with low heights on the left in the Northern Hemisphere.
Wind crossing isotherms: if wind blows from warm toward cold, there is warm advection. Cold toward warm is cold advection.
Dew point depression (temperature minus dew point): a small value (for example 3 C or less) means moist, probably cloud.
Closely spaced contours mean strong wind, and jets appear where speeds are highest.

lesson.note: Use 850 for temperature and precipitation type, 700 for moisture and ascent, 500 for the large-scale pattern, and 250 for the jet.

terms: Height of a pressure surface above sea level, adjusted for gravity variations.
Temperature minus dew point at a point.

questions.q: Which chart is most commonly used to identify steering flow, troughs and ridges?
c: 500 hPa
850 hPa
Surface chart
100 hPa
questions.e: The 500 hPa level is near the middle of the atmosphere's mass.

questions.q: Which chart is best for locating jet streams?
c: 250 hPa
850 hPa
700 hPa
Surface analysis
questions.e: 250 hPa is near the tropopause where jets are strongest.

questions.q: 850 hPa charts are especially useful for:
c: Low-level temperature advection and precipitation type
Locating the jet stream core and upper-level divergence
Measuring stratospheric ozone and tropopause height
Finding the position of the tropopause break aloft
questions.e: They show low-level temperatures and the 0 C line.

questions.q: If wind blows across isotherms from warm toward cold, what is occurring?
c: Warm air advection
Cold air advection
No advection
Frontolysis
questions.e: Warm air is being carried toward colder air.

questions.q: A small dew point depression on a 700 hPa chart suggests:
c: Moist air, likely cloud
Very dry air
Strong winds
A temperature inversion at 700 hPa only
questions.e: Small T minus Td means near saturation.

questions.q: 850 hPa charts are most useful for:
c: Low-level temperature advection and moisture
The jet stream core winds and tropopause height
Ozone levels and the height of the tropopause
Fog and visibility near the surface at each station
questions.e: 850 hPa is about 1.5 km.

questions.q: 500 hPa charts show height contours in:
c: Decametres
Hectopascals
Knots
Degrees
questions.e: 500 hPa heights are in dam (e.g., 552).

questions.q: The jet stream is best identified on the:
c: 250 hPa chart
850 hPa chart
1000 hPa chart
Surface chart
questions.e: 250 hPa corresponds to jet level.

questions.q: Typical 500 hPa height in mid-latitudes is around:
questions.e: 500 hPa is about 18,000 ft ASL (NAV CANADA guide), roughly 5,500 m.

questions.q: The 700 hPa level is commonly used to assess:
c: Mid-level moisture and vertical motion
Sea level pressure and the position of surface fronts
Ground temperature and visibility at the surface
Fog formation and low cloud near the ground
questions.e: 700 hPa is near 3 km.

questions.q: Temperature on 850 hPa of 0 C helps estimate:
c: Rain or snow potential in the lower atmosphere
Hail size in a thunderstorm and the strength of the updraft
Visibility and the cloud colour at each station
The height of the tropopause and the jet stream position
questions.e: 850 hPa temperatures are used for precipitation-type guidance.

sources: NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): constant pressure charts at 00Z and 12Z; 850 hPa 5,000 ft, 700 hPa 10,000 ft, 500 hPa 18,000 ft, 250 hPa 34,000 ft ASL; contour spacing and wind speed
unverified: Chart-reading tips (advection, dew point depression, use of each level) are standard practice, not checked in a fetched source.

topics.title: Numerical weather prediction (GEM, GFS, ECMWF) and limitations
lesson: Numerical weather prediction (NWP) solves the equations of fluid motion and thermodynamics on a grid to forecast the atmosphere. Forecasters use model output as guidance, not as the final answer.

list: GEM (Global Environmental Multiscale model): ECCC's atmospheric model. The Global Deterministic Prediction System (GDPS) runs at about 15 km out to 10 days, twice a day. The High Resolution Deterministic Prediction System (HRDPS Continental) runs at about 2.5 km over most of Canada out to 48 hours, up to four times a day.
GFS: the US National Weather Service global model.
ECMWF: the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Widely regarded as one of the most skillful global models.

lesson: Resolutions and run schedules change as models are upgraded. The ECCC figures above were read from ECCC's data catalogue on 2026-10-26. Check the current documentation.

list: Chaos: tiny errors in the starting state grow over time, so forecast skill falls with lead time. Little skill is expected beyond about two weeks.
Parameterization: processes smaller than the grid (convection, cloud microphysics, turbulence) are approximated.
Resolution: coarse models smooth out small features. A high-resolution model can resolve thunderstorms, terrain effects and sea breezes better, but it can also be wrong in more detail.
Initial conditions: observations are limited, especially over oceans.

lesson: An ensemble runs the model many times with slightly different starting conditions or physics. The spread among members shows uncertainty. Tight agreement means higher confidence. Large spread means low confidence and several possible outcomes.

lesson.note: Never rely on one model run. Compare models, check trends from run to run, and use ensembles to judge confidence.

terms: Representation of processes too small to resolve on the model grid.
Set of forecasts from slightly different starting conditions or physics.

questions.q: Which operational weather model is run by Canada's ECCC?
c: GEM
GFS
ECMWF IFS
UKMO Unified Model
questions.e: The Global Environmental Multiscale (GEM) model is ECCC's atmospheric model; ECCC's Meteorological Service of Canada produces its forecasts.

questions.q: Why does forecast skill decrease with lead time?
c: Small initial errors grow because the atmosphere is chaotic
Satellites gradually lose accuracy as the forecast period grows
Observations are removed from the model after the first day
Computers become slower as the model runs further ahead in time
questions.e: Chaotic growth of small errors limits predictability.

questions.q: What is the purpose of ensemble forecasting?
c: To estimate forecast uncertainty from multiple runs
To replace all observations with model data at the initial time
To raise the model resolution everywhere without extra cost
To remove all errors from the forecast at long lead times
questions.e: Spread among members indicates how confident to be.

questions.q: Why are parameterizations needed in NWP?
c: Some processes are smaller than the model grid
Observations are not available for the whole globe
Satellite data cannot be used in the model equations
The equations of motion are not known for large-scale flow
questions.e: Convection, microphysics and turbulence cannot be resolved directly and are approximated.

questions.q: If ensemble members disagree widely, forecast confidence should be:
c: Low
High
Unaffected
Equal to climatology only
questions.e: Large spread shows the forecast is sensitive and uncertain.

questions.q: The GEM model is run by:
c: Environment and Climate Change Canada
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts
The UK Met Office in Exeter, England
questions.e: GEM stands for Global Environmental Multiscale model. It is the atmospheric model used in ECCC's prediction systems.

questions.q: A model ensemble is a set of forecasts that:
c: Start from slightly different conditions
Use identical starting data and give identical results
Use only observations from the last hour at the surface
Use satellite data only, with no model physics at all
questions.e: Ensembles represent forecast uncertainty.

questions.q: Model resolution refers to:
c: Grid spacing
Time of run
Number of stations
Data format
questions.e: Finer grids resolve smaller features.

questions.q: Model output statistics (MOS) are used to:
c: Correct systematic model biases
Run the model at a finer grid than the global run
Draw fronts and pressure centres on a surface chart
Measure the wind speed and direction at a station
questions.e: MOS uses statistics to calibrate model output.

questions.q: A limitation of NWP is:
c: Chaos and initial condition errors grow with time
Models contain no physics and cannot represent clouds
Models predict perfectly out to ten days at all scales
Models use only one variable, so errors never grow
questions.e: Small errors amplify, limiting predictability.

questions.q: What is the horizontal resolution of ECCC's HRDPS (continental) as listed in ECCC's data catalogue?
c: About 2.5 km
About 15 km
About 50 km
About 100 m
questions.e: ECCC's data catalogue lists HRDPS Continental at about 2.5 km, up to 48 hours, up to four runs a day. The global system (GDPS) is 15 km. Resolutions change with upgrades.

sources: ECCC data catalogue (WIS2), HRDPS Continental: about 2.5 km, up to 48 h, up to four runs per day
ECCC data catalogue (WIS2), GDPS: 15 km, 10 days, twice a day, GEM as the atmosphere component
unverified: GFS and ECMWF descriptions, the ensemble and limitation points, and the 'about two weeks' predictability limit are general knowledge, not checked in a fetched source.

topics.title: Forecast verification and persistence
lesson: Verification checks how good forecasts are. It guides improvement and shows when to trust or discount a source.

list: Persistence: assume tomorrow will be like today. Very hard to beat for the first few hours in some elements, and a useful baseline.
Climatology: use the long-term average for the date. A baseline for longer ranges.

lesson.h: Yes/no event scores (from a contingency table)

list: Hits: event forecast and occurred. Misses: not forecast but occurred. False alarms: forecast but did not occur. Correct negatives: neither.
Probability of detection (POD) = hits / (hits + misses).
False alarm ratio (FAR) = false alarms / (hits + false alarms).
Critical success index (CSI) = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms).
Bias: average error. Shows consistent over or under forecasting.
Mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE): size of typical errors. RMSE penalizes big misses more.

lesson.formula: Skill = (score - reference score) / (perfect score - reference score)

lesson: A positive skill score means the forecast beat the reference. Zero means no better. Negative means worse.
For rare events, a forecast of 'no' every day is right most of the time but has no use. Use POD, FAR and CSI for rare events.

lesson.note: Verify against what matters to the user: thresholds like ceiling below 1,000 ft, not just average temperature error.

terms: Forecast that current conditions will continue.

questions.q: What is a persistence forecast?
c: A forecast that conditions will stay the same as now
A forecast built from the long-term average for the date
A forecast made by averaging an ensemble of model runs
A forecast produced by extrapolating radar echoes forward
questions.e: Persistence assumes no change from the current state.

questions.q: How is probability of detection (POD) calculated?
c: Hits / (hits + misses)
False alarms / (hits + false alarms)
Hits / (hits + false alarms)
Misses / total
questions.e: POD is the fraction of observed events that were forecast.

questions.q: How is the false alarm ratio (FAR) calculated?
c: False alarms / (hits + false alarms)
Hits / (hits + misses)
Misses / (hits + misses)
Correct negatives / total
questions.e: FAR is the fraction of forecast events that did not occur.

questions.q: A positive skill score means the forecast:
c: Beat the reference forecast
Was perfect
Was worse than persistence
Had no errors
questions.e: Skill is improvement over a chosen reference.

questions.q: Why can 'percent correct' be misleading for rare events like tornadoes?
c: Always forecasting 'no' can score very high while being useless
The score cannot be computed when events are uncommon
It gives too much weight to forecasts of false alarms
It ignores correct negatives and so exaggerates rare events
questions.e: Rare events make correct negatives dominate the score.

questions.q: Persistence forecasting assumes:
c: Future weather will be the same as current
Weather is random, so no forecast beats chance
Weather always changes within the next six hours
Models are perfect, so persistence adds nothing
questions.e: Persistence is a basic benchmark.

questions.q: A forecast has 40 hits, 10 misses and 20 false alarms. What is the probability of detection (POD)?
questions.e: POD = hits / (hits + misses) = 40/50 = 0.80.

questions.q: Using hits 40, misses 10, false alarms 20, what is the false alarm ratio (FAR)?
questions.e: FAR = false alarms / (hits + false alarms) = 20/60 = 0.33.

questions.q: Using hits 40, misses 10, false alarms 20, what is the critical success index (CSI)?
questions.e: CSI = hits / (hits + misses + false alarms) = 40/70 = 0.57.

questions.q: Forecast errors of +2, -1, +3, 0 degrees give a bias of:
c: +1.0 degrees
+6 degrees
0 degrees
-1.0 degrees
questions.e: Bias is the mean error: (2-1+3+0)/4 = 1.0.

questions.q: Forecast errors of +2, -1, +3, 0 degrees give a mean absolute error (MAE) of:
c: 1.5 degrees
1.0 degrees
6 degrees
0.5 degrees

sources: NWS Glossary of Forecast Verification Metrics: POD, FAR, bias, MAE, RMSE, skill score, persistence and climatology as reference forecasts
unverified: The CSI formula (hits / (hits + misses + false alarms)) is standard but was not stated in the source that was read.
